name: Aaron Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the power company's hill depot, keeping the lines up through the valleys and up the ridges where the roads turn to gravel. A normal day, we load the trucks at seven, say a quick word together, and head out to whatever's broken or due for replacing. Some poles up there you can't reach with a bucket truck, so you climb them with spikes and a belt, the old way. I love that, honestly, it's a craft. What wears me out is the drive, two hours there and back on bad roads, and winter, when the snow takes lines down faster than we can fix them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I understand you train the apprentices too. How did that start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The depot manager asked me ten years ago because I'm patient and I don't cut corners. I teach them climbing, rigging, how to read a line, and mostly how not to die. I'm proud of every one who's come through, there's eleven of them working now. I'm also a deacon at our church, so between the two I'm used to being the one people come to. Pay's lower up here than in the cities, and there's no other line work in these hills, so my wife Priya runs a small childcare from our home to help with the mortgage. We get by, but there's nothing extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People get excited about every new gadget, and in the end you still need a man who knows what he's doing. I'd say it after church, probably, over coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be glad. I don't use these AI things and I don't want to. I like my work the way it is, and I want my apprentices to learn it the right way, by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep training the young ones, keep working, keep putting what little we can aside. Same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want the apprentices to learn the right way. What's the wrong way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them want to look everything up on a phone. A lad last year asked a chat program how to rig a pole and it gave him rubbish, the kind of thing that gets you killed. I told him, you learn it from your hands and from me, not from a machine that's never touched a wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'what little we can aside'. How much is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months nothing. We've maybe two weeks of money saved. Priya's childcare is steady but small, and with two kids and the mortgage, it goes. We trust God and work hard, and so far we've managed.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people get excited about every new gadget and you still need a man who knows what he's doing. I'd say it over coffee after church.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I don't use AI and don't want to. I like my work as it is and want my apprentices to learn it properly, by hand.
S0.do: Carries on training apprentices by hand and working the hill lines as before. Keeps putting aside what little the family can, which some months is nothing.
S0.quote: You learn it from your hands and from me, not from a machine that's never touched a wire.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is a proud craftsman, apprentice trainer and church deacon whose identity rests on passing on skill by hand. His distrust of AI was reinforced by an apprentice getting dangerous advice from a chatbot. Money is tight, with about two weeks of savings, and his faith is part of how he copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not all bad, but people need to be careful. Work is good for a man, and if machines take too much of it, families suffer. I'd say young people should still learn real trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job holds, for now at least. These hills are too rough for fancy machines. But I'd worry about the apprenticeships. If the company decides it needs fewer people, the training's the first thing they cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait to see what the company does. I'd fight to keep the apprenticeship programme going, talk to the depot manager, maybe write to head office. I wouldn't learn the new tools unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a storm on the horizon that might pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would losing the apprenticeships bother you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's how the trade lives. I learned from an old lineman named Walter, who learned from his father. If they stop training young ones, in twenty years there's nobody who knows how to climb a pole in a storm. A trade isn't just a job, it's handed down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if they cut the programme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the city offices who've never been up a pole. They look at a spreadsheet and see a cost. And the tech companies selling them the idea that a machine can replace a man's judgement. They're the ones I'd blame.

S1.say: I'd say it isn't all bad but people should be careful, because work is good for a man and families suffer if machines take too much. Young people should still learn real trades.
S1.think: I think my job holds for now, since the hills are too rough for fancy machines. But I'd worry the company would cut the apprenticeships first if it needed fewer people.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what the company does, while fighting to keep the apprenticeship programme by lobbying the depot manager and head office. Avoids new tools unless required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm on the horizon that might pass.
S1.quote: A trade isn't just a job, it's handed down.
S1.fieldNote: His main worry is the apprenticeship programme, which he sees as the trade's lifeline. He blames city office staff and tech companies, not workers or government. His traditional values show in how he talks about work as good for a man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a dark day, and people need to look after each other. Families and churches will have to step up. I'd say the government shouldn't just hand out money, it should help people find work, any work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be very frightened. If robots can climb poles in two years, there's nothing for me. Two weeks' savings, a mortgage, and no other work in these hills. I don't know computers, and I'm too old to start over in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back right away, everything that's not food, heat or the mortgage. I'd lean on the church and my brothers, and I'd take any work going, cutting firewood, building fences, fixing roofs, whatever pays. If the government offered help, I'd take it to feed my kids, but it would eat at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, and ashamed of being afraid. I'd pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it would eat at you to take government help. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father never took a penny from anyone. He worked until his back gave out. Taking help feels like failing my family. But I wouldn't let my children go hungry for my pride. I'd just hate every day of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that I don't know what's coming. I'd tell them to stick together, look after their families, and not lose faith. And I'd tell them that the skills they learned still matter, even if a robot does the job, because a man who can work with his hands can always find something.

S2.say: I'd call it a dark day and say families and churches must look after each other. I'd say government shouldn't just hand out money but help people find any work.
S2.think: I'd be very frightened, since robots climbing poles in two years leaves nothing for me. With two weeks' savings, a mortgage and no other work in the hills, I'm too old to start over in two years.
S2.do: Cuts everything but food, heat and the mortgage and leans on his church and brothers. Takes any work going, like cutting firewood, fencing or roofing, and would accept government help only to feed his children.
S2.feel: Afraid and ashamed of being afraid, praying a lot.
S2.quote: Taking help feels like failing my family. But I wouldn't let my children go hungry for my pride.
S2.fieldNote: Faith and pride shape his response, and he'd lean on church and family before government. The tension between his values and his need was the most honest moment. He still believes manual skills matter, even in a world of robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and wise people prepare. I'd tell young men to keep working hard and save, and to learn a trade robots can't do, if there is one. I'd say churches and communities should start getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives us a little time to save, maybe pay off the car. But I still don't see what I'd do after. I'm a lineman. I'm not going to become something else at forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save every bit we can, cut out the small things now. I'd keep working and keep training apprentices as long as they let me. I'd try to put some money into Priya's childcare, maybe expand it a little, since people will always want a person to watch their children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think childcare is safer than line work. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you leave your baby with a robot? I wouldn't. People want a person who loves their child. Priya's good at it, the parents trust her. If we could take in a couple more children, it could carry us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't become something else at forty-eight. Is that fear or choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'm scared of starting over, I won't lie. But I also believe God gave me this work. If it ends, I'll do what I must, but I won't go looking for a new life before the old one's finished.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a warning and wise people prepare, so young men should work hard, save and learn a trade robots can't do. Churches and communities should start getting ready.
S3.think: Five years gives us time to save and maybe pay off the car, but I don't see what I'd do after. I'm a lineman and won't become something else at forty-eight.
S3.do: Saves every bit, cuts small expenses and keeps working and training apprentices as long as allowed. Invests a little in expanding his wife's home childcare, believing people will always want a person to look after children.
S3.feel: Anxious, but feeling he's doing something.
S3.quote: Would you leave your baby with a robot? I wouldn't.
S3.fieldNote: He uses the warning time to save and build up his wife's childcare business, which he sees as safe from robots. He's honest that fear and faith both keep him from planning a career change. He wants to finish the life he has before starting a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to prepare if people are sensible. Work hard, save, keep your family close. I'd say communities should look after their own, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is easier. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, maybe the mortgage nearly paid. I could keep working until near the end and then, I don't know. It's still the end of my trade, and that's hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save steadily and pay extra on the mortgage. I'd keep working and training apprentices for as long as there's a programme. I'd talk to Ravi about his future, maybe steer him away from line work, which would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but it feels further off. There's time to pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fourteen and he's been asking about becoming a lineman like me. I'd tell him I'm proud he wants to, but the trade might not be there when he's my age. Maybe something with people, a nurse or a teacher. It'd hurt, but I'd rather tell him now than watch him lose it later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the ten-year picture you feel hopeful about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my children would be grown and settled before it hits. That's the main thing. And maybe in ten years, people will remember that work matters, that a man needs to be useful. If we lose that, we lose more than jobs.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to prepare if people are sensible, working hard, saving and keeping family close. Communities should look after their own rather than wait for government.
S4.think: Ten years is easier, since I'd be fifty-three with grown kids and maybe a nearly paid mortgage. It's still the end of my trade, and that's hard.
S4.do: Saves steadily, pays extra on the mortgage and keeps working and training apprentices while the programme lasts. Talks with his son about steering away from line work.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but it feels further off, with time to pray on it.
S4.quote: It'd hurt, but I'd rather tell him now than watch him lose it later.
S4.fieldNote: The decade's main gift for him is that his children would be grown first. Steering his son away from the trade he loves was a painful choice. He worries about losing the dignity of work, not only income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With two weeks' savings and nothing else in these hills, we'd be in real trouble. What would help is work, real work, maybe training for jobs that still need people, and the church and families pulling together. Not handouts, but a hand up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of men like me, our work is part of who we are before God. If that's taken away, it's not just money we lose. You'd have a lot of men sitting at home wondering what they're for.

headlineQuote: You'd have a lot of men sitting at home wondering what they're for.
portrait: Aaron Patel is a 43-year-old lineworker in a hill-country depot who still climbs poles with spikes, trains the company's apprentices and serves as a deacon at his church. His wife runs a small home childcare to help with the mortgage, and with two kids they have about two weeks of savings. He's traditional, distrusts government handouts and has never used AI tools, preferring to learn and teach by hand. He's calm if AI plateaus, uneasy that steady change would cut apprenticeships, alarmed by two-year AGI and anxious with five or ten years, when he'd save, lean on his church and family, and put hope in his wife's childcare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because with two weeks of savings and no other work in the hills, his family would be in real trouble.
whatWouldHelp: Real work and training for jobs that still need people, and churches and families pulling together. A hand up, not a handout.
